newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain, France may send rapid aid force to Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Spain, France may send rapid aid force to Zaire.

text.p: Spain and France may send a U.N.-approved rapid deployment force to aid refugees in Zaire ahead of a relief operation organised by the United Nations, Spanish defence ministry officials said on Monday.
Defence Minister Eduardo Serra said troops were on alert for the possibility of immediate intervention in Zaire.
He said the U.N. Security Council was trying to mobilise its own military force to secure humanitarian corridors for distribution of aid to more than a million refugees.
"But there is a chance of sending before that a multinational force, and we are now making efforts for its organisation and dispatch, as quickly and as urgently as possible," Serra said.

A defence ministry spokesman told Reuters the U.N. might approve a multinational force which could be assembled quickly and sent ahead of a task force actually organised by the U.N. which could take a month.
"The United Nations is going to send its own task force but before, with more urgency, the U.N. may allow the dispatch of a rapid force," the spokesman said. "It may only be Spain and France."
Spain would not send any troops before the United Nations gave its approval, however, the spokesman said.
He said Spain was prepared immediately to send 300 soldiers in an initial deployment and was still considering whether it would send more in later stages of the operation.

On Saturday, the U.N. Security Council called on member states to lay the groundwork for a multinational force to help end the crisis in eastern Zaire but postponed its deployment until a later stage.

"Spain understands it is urgent to intervene," said Serra. "Spain has given urgent orders to make preparations and alert our troops in anticipation that it will be possible" to deploy them immediately, he added.
Spain has backed France in spearheading efforts for immediate deployment of such a force to Zaire.

The U.N. Security Council on Saturday gave Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, a strong supporter of a multinational force, until November 20 to report on the framework and operations of such a venture.

The council's failure to authorise immediate deployment angered the European Union's commissioner for humanitarian aid, Emma Bonino, who accused the U.N. of not caring about the fate of thousands of refugees in Zaire.
Boutros-Ghali said on Sunday thousands were dying by the hour.

The Spanish defence ministry spokesman said the exact destination of the force in Africa had not yet been decided. Other Spanish officials have mentioned the eastern Zaire town of Kindu as a possible launching point.

The United States, cool to the idea of a multinational force, said on Monday it had seen no coherent plans for one and did not know what the scope of the force would be or who was going to pay for it.
Britain has also said it was unlikely to send troops.
